candidates.original_title: Learning about what others were doing: Verb aspect and attributions of mundane and criminal intent for past actions
candidates.description: Describing criminal actions in the imperfective aspect causes participants to attribute greater intentionality to the perpetrator than describing the same actions in the perfective aspect.
candidates.citation_sentence: In the Kurby and Kibbe study, participants read the original, unaltered vignette used by Hart and Albarracín (2011, see Appendix A), and they also had access to the vignette while making their ratings.
candidates.notes: The registered replication report combined 11 laboratory replications and one MTurk replication of Experiment 3; the aggregate replication did not support the original criminal-intentionality effect. A follow-up direct replication using the unaltered vignette also found no significant effect. [luna56: extra entry, not in the external record]

candidates.original_title: Learning about what others were doing: Verb aspect and attributions of mundane and criminal intent for past actions
candidates.description: Describing criminal actions in the imperfective aspect makes them easier to imagine and promotes more detailed processing than describing the same actions in the perfective aspect.
candidates.citation_sentence: In the Kurby and Kibbe study, participants read the original, unaltered vignette used by Hart and Albarracín (2011, see Appendix A), and they also had access to the vignette while making their ratings.
candidates.notes: The aggregate replication found no evidence that imperfective aspect increased detailed processing or imagery. The follow-up direct replication also found no significant effect. [luna56: extra entry, not in the external record]
